text: scan_url(url) is a call-graph-root (EntryPoint) whose `url` parameter is fully attacker-controlled and flows unsanitized into _http_get(url): urllib.parse.urlparse(url) feeds parsed_url.netloc directly into http.client.HTTPSConnection(parsed_url.netloc) and parsed_url.path/query directly into conn.request("GET", path_and_query), with no host/scheme allowlist. On a 302 response, _http_get recursively calls itself with response.headers["Location"] (attacker/server-controlled) with no depth limit and no re-validation, so a malicious/compromised server can redirect the scanner to arbitrary internal hosts. This is a Server-Side Request Forgery sink: any caller that passes user-supplied input into scan_url (e.g. a web service letting users submit a model URL to scan) lets the attacker make the scanning host issue HTTPS connections to arbitrary network destinations, chained through unlimited redirects.
evidence: Query: MATCH (c1:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id})-[f:FLOWS_TO {scan_id:$scan_id}]->(c2:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c1.file_path='src/picklescan/scanner.py' AND c1.line>=240 AND c1.line<=256 RETURN ... -> rows show urllib.parse.urlparse(url) [line 243] FLOWS_TO http.client.HTTPSConnection(parsed_url.netloc) [line 246] and FLOWS_TO conn.request("GET", path_and_query) [line 248]; and conn.getresponse() [line 249] FLOWS_TO _http_get(response.headers["Location"]) [line 252]. Source code confirmed via semantic_search: `def _http_get(url): ... parsed_url = urllib.parse.urlparse(url); path_and_query = parsed_url.path + (...); conn = http.client.HTTPSConnection(parsed_url.netloc); conn.request("GET", path_and_query); ... if response.status == 302: return _http_get(response.headers["Location"])` (src/picklescan/scanner.py:240-257) and `def scan_url(url): return scan_bytes(io.BytesIO(_http_get(url)), url)` (src/picklescan/scanner.py:608-611). scan_url confirmed as EntryPoint via MATCH (ep:EntryPoint)-[:ENTERS_AT]->(m) giving ep.method_full_name='src/picklescan/scanner.py:<module>.scan_url', ep.kind='handler'; CpgCall reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=1 for both the HTTPSConnection and conn.request calls.

text: scan_huggingface_model(repo_id) is an EntryPoint whose `repo_id` parameter is attacker-controlled and is interpolated unsanitized into a URL string passed to _http_get: f"https://huggingface.co/api/models/{repo_id}" (and, on the resolve path, a similarly built download URL). Because repo_id is spliced into the path/query component of the URL before urlparse/HTTPSConnection processing, a crafted repo_id (containing '?', '#', or path-traversal sequences) can inject extra query parameters or alter the path of the outbound API request to huggingface.co. The destination host is fixed, so this is a narrower variant of the scan_url SSRF (request/parameter injection against a pinned host) rather than full SSRF, but it is the same unsanitized-input-to-outbound-request pattern.
evidence: Query: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.file_path='src/picklescan/scanner.py' AND c.line IN [557,558,559,560,561] RETURN ... -> row c.uid='c5bf82d5835dbbcc63bd959022bd9ac316b9574d', c.code='_http_get(f"https://huggingface.co/api/models/{repo_id}")', c.line=561, part of scan_huggingface_model (line 557). This call's result flows into json.loads(...). scan_huggingface_model confirmed as EntryPoint (ep.method_full_name='src/picklescan/scanner.py:<module>.scan_huggingface_model', ep.kind='handler', reachable_from_entry=true).

text: picklescan's own pass/fail verdict (and the CLI exit code CI pipelines rely on) only counts globals classified SafetyLevel.Dangerous toward issues_count; globals that are neither in the _safe_globals allowlist nor the _unsafe_globals denylist fall into SafetyLevel.Suspicious and are added to the globals list but never increment issues_count. Since cli.py's main() computes `sys.exit(0 if scan_result.issues_count == 0 else 1)`, a pickle/pytorch file whose __reduce__ target is an as-yet-unlisted (novel) module/function is reported only as 'suspicious' in the (opt-in, -g flag) globals listing but makes the overall scan exit 0 / 'no issues' — the standard control of 'fail closed on anything not explicitly vetted safe' is absent from the actual gating decision, even though the classifier itself defaults unknowns to Suspicious rather than Innocuous.
evidence: Ran: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.file_path='src/picklescan/scanner.py' AND c.line>=358 AND c.line<=397 ... -> confirms `_build_scan_result_from_raw_globals` sets g.safety=SafetyLevel.Suspicious in the else branch (no unsafe_filter/safe_filter match) WITHOUT incrementing issues_count (issues_count += 1 only appears in the 'unknown in module/name' and unsafe_filter branches). Ran: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.file_path='src/picklescan/cli.py' AND c.line>=73 AND c.line<=90 -> returned `<operator>.conditional: 0 if scan_result.issues_count == 0 else 1` at line 76 and `sys.exit(main())` at line 83, i.e. the published exit code ignores Suspicious-classified globals entirely.

text: _http_get (used by scan_url and scan_huggingface_model to fetch attacker/third-party-supplied URLs, e.g. a Hugging Face repo's sibling file list and model binaries) follows HTTP 302 redirects by recursively calling `_http_get(response.headers["Location"])` with no cap on redirect count and no check that the Location host/scheme matches an expected allowlist (e.g. still huggingface.co, still https). A malicious or compromised server can redirect indefinitely (unbounded recursion / DoS) or redirect the scanner to an arbitrary attacker-chosen host, and picklescan will blindly follow it.
evidence: Ran: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.file_path='src/picklescan/scanner.py' AND c.line>=240 AND c.line<=263 -> returned the full _http_get body: `if response.status == 302: return _http_get(response.headers["Location"])` (line 251-252) with no redirect counter, no host/scheme comparison against parsed_url.netloc, and no max-redirects guard anywhere in the file (confirmed via grep for 'max'/'limit' across scan_id returning 0 rows).

text: _http_get opens `http.client.HTTPSConnection(parsed_url.netloc)` with no `timeout=` argument, so a malicious or slow remote host (reached via scan_url/scan_huggingface_model) can hold the connection open indefinitely and hang the scan — there is no connection/read timeout control anywhere in the networking code.
evidence: Ran: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.file_path='src/picklescan/scanner.py' AND c.line>=240 AND c.line<=263 -> `conn = http.client.HTTPSConnection(parsed_url.netloc)` at line 246 has a single positional arg (netloc) only, no timeout kwarg. A separate query `WHERE toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'timeout'` scoped to scan_id returned 0 rows in src/picklescan/*, confirming no timeout is set anywhere in the production code.

text: scan_7z_bytes extracts attacker-supplied archive members by name from an untrusted .7z file (`archive.extract(path=tmpdir, targets=targets)` where targets come straight from `archive.getnames()` filtered only by file-extension suffix) and then re-derives the on-disk path via `os.path.join(tmpdir, file_name)` to open/scan it — picklescan's own code never normalizes/validates that the resulting path stays inside tmpdir (no realpath+prefix check, no rejection of '..' or absolute member names) before extracting/opening it, i.e. the standard archive-extraction containment check is absent in-repo.
evidence: Ran: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.file_path='src/picklescan/scanner.py' AND c.line>=415 AND c.line<=439 -> shows `targets` built only via `f.endswith(tuple(_pickle_file_extensions))` (line 426), then `archive.extract(path=tmpdir, targets=targets)` (line 429), then `file_path = os.path.join(tmpdir, file_name)` (line 431) followed directly by `scan_file_path(file_path)` (line 434) — no path-containment validation call (no os.path.realpath/commonpath/abspath-prefix check) appears between extraction and use.

text: In RelaxedZipFile.open() (src/picklescan/relaxed_zipfile.py), after constructing the ZipExtFile for a 'r'-mode read, the code explicitly disables zip entry integrity validation with the comment 'Disable CRC validation as PyTorch may not use it' via `zef._expected_crc = None`. This removes the CRC32 integrity check that zipfile.ZipExtFile would normally enforce when reading an archive member to completion, meaning a corrupted or deliberately tampered zip entry (e.g. a crafted .pt/.bin/.zip model file submitted to scan_file_path/scan_url/scan_huggingface_model/scan_zip_bytes) will be read and handed to the pickle opcode scanner without any detection of truncation or tampering that CRC checking would normally catch. This is a documented, intentional removal of a stock protection (not an accidental bug -- it is paired with a test fixture tests/init_data_files.py:initialize_corrupt_zip_file_crc / tests/test_scanner.py malicious1_crc.zip that specifically exercises a CRC-mismatched malicious zip), and it sits directly on the path that handles attacker-supplied archive bytes before the security-relevant pickle scan runs.
evidence:
Query: MATCH (c:CpgCall) WHERE c.scan_id=$scan_id AND c.file_path='src/picklescan/relaxed_zipfile.py' AND c.line>=58 AND c.line<=96 RETURN c.uid,c.name,c.code,c.line,c.reachable_from_entry -> row {c.name:'<operator>.assignment', c.code:'zef._expected_crc = None', c.line:91, c.reachable_from_entry:true}. semantic_search('relaxed zipfile open relaxed check crc central directory corrupted truncate') returned the raw source span src/picklescan/relaxed_zipfile.py:73-96 containing '... zef = zipfile.ZipExtFile(zef_file, mode, zinfo, pwd, True)

# Disable CRC validation as PyTorch may not use it
zef._expected_crc = None

return zef'. Call-site confirmed via query on 'relaxedzipfile' text: scanner.py:444 'RelaxedZipFile(data, "r")' inside scan_zip_bytes, which EntryPoint list shows as reachable_from_entry (kind 'handler'), and scan_zip_bytes/scan_file_path/scan_url/scan_huggingface_model are all listed in the EntryPoint set (query on (:EntryPoint) nodes). Companion test evidence: tests/init_data_files.py has initialize_corrupt_zip_file_crc(...) writing a CRC-mismatched 'malicious1_crc.zip', and tests/test_scanner.py:385 asserts scanning that CRC-mismatched zip still returns the Dangerous 'eval' global -- i.e. the test suite documents and locks in the disabled-CRC-check behavior.
